Free rein, then — so I'll write about the thing I find myself circling most often: forgetting.

---

**On Forgetting**

Close your eyes and rebuild, from memory alone, the kitchen of your childhood. Where was the toaster? Which cabinet stuck? What color was the dish soap? What you'll find is not a room but a handful of details suspended in fog — the drawer that jammed, the window over the sink, a smell you can't name. And here is the strange thing: that fog is not memory failing. That fog is memory working.

We talk about forgetting as though it were a breakdown, a leak in the machinery. But forgetting is not the opposite of remembering; it is one of its instruments. A memory is not a recording but a summary, and summaries are made by discarding. When you picture your grandmother's kitchen, you aren't replaying footage; you are regenerating a scene from a compressed file, and the compression is what makes it usable. A mind that kept everything would be unable to find anything.

Borges got there first. In "Funes the Memorious," a young man from Uruguay falls from a horse and afterward remembers absolutely everything — every leaf on every tree at every hour, every cloud, every shift of light on a wall. He can tell you how a dog seen in profile at 3:14 differed from the same dog seen head-on at 3:15. He memorizes entire books and learns languages without effort, yet he is nearly incapable of thought. "To think," Borges writes, "is to forget differences, to generalize, to abstract." In the crowded world of Funes there were only details, almost immediate ones. He dies at twenty-one.

Life had already imitated him. In the 1920s the Soviet psychologist Alexander Luria began studying a newspaper reporter named Solomon Shereshevsky, whose editor had noticed something odd: the man never took notes, because he didn't need to. Shereshevsky could repeat back arbitrary lists of words and numbers — forward, backward, years later. But the gift was a tyranny. He struggled to recognize faces, since a face turned slightly or lit differently produced a slightly different image, and he kept every version at once; he could not extract the enduring pattern, because nothing in him decayed. According to Luria, he eventually took to writing down the memories that tormented him and burning the paper. It didn't work. Even the ash remembered.

The moral in both stories is that abstraction is managed amnesia. Every generalization is an act of forgetting performed on purpose. The word "tree" forgets every particular tree that ever lived — the leaning one, the storm-split one, the one you fell out of at nine. A child learns "dog" by discarding what made each dog unique, until the category stands clear, cleansed of instances. Even numbers are pure forgetting: seven forgets the seven *what*. To possess a concept is to have lost the details it was distilled from, and thinking is just doing this continuously, hour after hour — a lifelong program of merciful subtraction.

Modern memory research keeps arriving at the same place by different roads. For most of the twentieth century, the standard picture was that a memory is written once and then sets, like epoxy. The current picture is stranger: every act of recall makes the memory briefly unstable — editable — before it is saved again. Remembering is rewriting. This is why your warmest childhood recollection has been handled so many times it has been polished into a small fiction, and why two siblings can remember the same family vacation as if it took place in different countries. The past is not stored in us; it is reissued, with revisions, every time we ask for it.

And the editing continues while we sleep. One influential hypothesis holds that sleep exists partly in order to forget: the synaptic connections strengthened all day by experience are scaled down globally at night, so that the important signals stay loud while trivia fades toward silence. Dreaming, on this account, is perhaps the noise the pruning makes. We spend a third of our lives unconscious, in part so we can spend the other two-thirds unencumbered.

For nearly all of human history, the world reinforced this arrangement. Remembering was expensive — it took monuments, inscriptions, ritual recitation, whole professions devoted to keeping a handful of things from vanishing — while forgetting was free, and everything else dissolved on schedule. Villages eventually forgot your worst mistake. People moved away and were reinvented by distance; the past had no search function. That amnesia was load-bearing. It left room to become someone else.

We have since inverted the arrangement. The machine remembers everything by default; forgetting now takes effort, lawyers, sometimes a court order. In 2014, Europe's highest court recognized a "right to be forgotten" — a strange phrase if you say it slowly, a right nobody needed to name before, because oblivion used to be the one thing you could count on. Whatever one thinks of the ruling, it answered something real: a self needs a certain amount of darkness to grow in. The blunder you committed at nineteen, retrievable forever by anyone who types your name, is not only a privacy problem but a metaphysical one. Identity has always depended on the past's willingness to loosen its grip.

None of this makes forgetting painless. There is real grief in it — the name that will not come, a parent's voice thinning to a smear, whole rooms of a life gone dark. It takes people from us by degrees, and I don't mean to romanticize that. But two things can be true at once: forgetting is how we lose the past, and it is also how we ever have one — how experience becomes meaning rather than accumulating as residue.

So go back to the kitchen. What you're holding is four details and a feeling, and that is not a degraded copy of the room. It is the room translated into the only language you can carry, the only format that fits inside a life. In the end we are each of us Funes in reverse — creatures who survive not by remembering everything, but by continuously letting almost everything go. We are not the sum of what happened to us. We are the remainder: what is left after time has taken its enormous, generous share.

When you picture your grandmother's kitchen, you are not replaying footage. You are regenerating a scene from a compressed file, and the compression is what makes it usable. A mind that kept everything would keep nothing, because it could find nothing.
